wrong: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away. | right: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.
wrong: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away. | right: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday reading: 'println' is just 'print', and 'new line' is something you do before writing. Java rule: println(x) prints x and then ends the line; println() alone just ends the line.
[1] misconception (M) -> PrintEqualsPrintln: wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
[2] misconception (M) -> PrintNewLineFirst: wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PrintEqualsPrintln: Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
[4] misconception (M) -> IdentifierCaseInsensitive: wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
[5] misconception (M) -> ParenthesesOnlyIfArgument: wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

[0] names_the_element (N): System.out.println is a library method that prints its argument followed by a line terminator ('print line').
[1] states_the_rule (S): println(String x) behaves as though it calls print(x) and then println(); println() terminates the current line by writing the line separator string.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Evaluate the argument, print its characters at the current position, then write the line separator so the cursor moves to the beginning of the next line.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Output is the value's characters followed by a line break: println("Hello, "); println("World!"); prints two lines.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One call appends the text and a line separator to the output; the cursor ends at the start of the next line; no variable changes and nothing is returned.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): System.out.println(s); is a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): print leaves the cursor on the line; println ends it; several prints followed by one println make one line.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): println prints numbers with all their digits and always ends the line; printf formats each value by its conversion code and ends the line only where the format has %n or \n.
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: produce one complete line of output, e.g. each result on its own line, or end a line built with print.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PrintEqualsPrintln: Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use println when each output item belongs on its own line or to end a line; use print to continue a line and printf to control number formatting.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Finish a line of print calls with println. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: output ends with print, so the last line may not be shown or runs into the shell prompt
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Method names are case-sensitive. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: System.out.Println or system.out.println: cannot find symbol
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Calls need parentheses. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: System.out.println; without ()

print leaves the cursor on the same line after printing; println moves the cursor to the next line after printing.
println prints each number with all its digits and ends the line; printf formats each value by its conversion code and starts a new line only when \n is in the format string.
println of an array variable prints the array's reference, not its elements.
System.out.println(s); is itself a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.
